extracted.intended_audience: IP office staff, policymakers, IP/statistics researchers and industrial design practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, counting conventions and procedural metrics used to evaluate industrial design applications and registrations worldwide (WIPO statistical guidance and definitions). Useful for compiling, comparing and interpreting industrial-design-related statistics and eligibility outcomes across offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial design eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: In general, for an industrial design to be eligible for protection, it typically needs to meet criteria such as being new, original and of an individual character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examination procedures vary widely between offices; some offices do substantive examination of novelty/originality while others do not. The phrasing 'typically needs' indicates these are the common substantive thresholds applied by many offices, but local law may vary in detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive examination practice
rubrics_metrics.description: At some offices, no search is made and no examination as to substance is carried out prior to registration. At other offices, a substantive examination is conducted, whereby the design is checked against designs on the register for novelty and/or originality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural difference affects registration rates, pendency and the meaning of 'registered' across offices. When comparing offices, note whether substantive examination is performed and whether searches are conducted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application design count (designs contained in applications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistics based on the number of designs contained in industrial design applications – known as application design counts – improve comparability worldwide by harmonizing data between offices that allow several designs to be contained within a single application and those that allow only one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use application design counts to compare offices with multiple-design application systems to those with single-design systems. The report uses design counts (not just application counts) to mitigate differences arising from filing-system rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent design count for regional offices
rubrics_metrics.description: Designs in applications filed at some regional offices are equivalent to multiple designs in applications filed in the respective member states of those offices. To calculate the number of equivalent designs for the OAPI (17 member states), the Benelux Office for Intellectual Property (BOIP) (3) and the EUIPO (27), each design is multiplied by the corresponding number of member states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This multiplication is applied to produce 'equivalent' counts for comparability. Note exceptions: ARIPO and EAPO do not register designs with automatic region‑wide applicability and are treated differently (see separate rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent application counting for ARIPO and EAPO
rubrics_metrics.description: The African Regional Intellectual Property Organization (ARIPO) and the Eurasian Patent Organization (EAPO) do not register industrial designs with an automatic region-wide applicability. Therefore, for these offices, each application is counted as one application abroad if the applicant does not reside within a member state, or as one resident application and one application abroad if the applicant resides within a member state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This specific counting convention differs from how EUIPO/BOIP/OAPI equivalent counts are handled and must be applied when producing comparable origin/office statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resident vs non-resident / origin definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications received by offices from resident and non-resident applicants are referred to as office data, whereas applications filed by applicants at their home office(s) (resident applications) or at foreign offices (applications abroad) are referred to as origin data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The origin of an industrial design application is determined by the residence of the first named applicant. For regional offices, an application filed at a regional office is considered resident if the applicant resides in one of that office's member states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting and comparability caveats
rubrics_metrics.description: Every effort has been made to compile procedural data based on common definitions and concepts, but procedural differences make it extremely difficult to fully harmonize such data. Therefore, caution should be exercised when making comparisons across offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The total number of applications processed for a given office may be incomplete owing to the omission of one or several elements by the office. '..' indicates not available. Analysts should treat cross-office comparisons and growth rates cautiously and inspect national counting rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: China data counting change (post-2017)
rubrics_metrics.description: From 2017 onwards, industrial design application data provided by the IP office of China include only those applications for which the necessary application fees has been paid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because China accounts for most of the global total, this change means it is not possible to report the 2017 worldwide application growth rate directly; analysts must account for the counting change when interpreting trends and world totals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing routes: Paris route vs Hague System
rubrics_metrics.description: World totals include applications filed directly with national and regional offices (known as the Paris route), as well as the designations received via the Hague System (where applicable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Hague System is treated as a distinct filing route and accounted for in non-resident filing shares (e.g., ~33.8% of global non-resident filing activity in 2022). Changes in filing-route shares can substantially affect office-level non-resident counts (e.g., post-Brexit UK direct filings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial design right duration
rubrics_metrics.description: Industrial design rights generally last for up to 15 years from the date an application is filed, although they last up to 25 years in most European countries and up to 10 years in China.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different maximum terms across jurisdictions affect counts of 'registrations in force' and the average age of active registrations; comparisons should account for term variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pendency and processing time metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Key procedural metrics include number of examiners (FTE), days to first office action (from filing) and days to final office decision. Potentially pending applications are all industrial design applications, at any stage in the process, awaiting a final decision by an office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These metrics vary widely across offices (e.g., EUIPO processes applications in under five days on average; Thailand had much longer averages). Use consistent definitions (first office action days, final decision days) when comparing offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination outcome categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Industrial design examination outcomes are categorized as registered, total rejections, withdrawn or abandoned, and applications pending (potentially pending).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distribution of outcomes differs widely by office (examples: EUIPO registered 96.7% of processed applications in 2022; US had 23.7% rejected). Outcome shares reflect both substantive law and procedural practices (e.g., whether substantive examination is performed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grouping by Locarno classes into industry sectors
rubrics_metrics.description: Grouping the 32 Locarno classes into 12 industry sectors serves to highlight the most important industry sectors for designs contained within industrial design applications filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sector grouping is a methodological choice used to present which industries dominate design filings (e.g., furniture & household goods, textiles & accessories, tools & machines, electricity & lighting accounted for majority share).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjusting design counts by GDP and population (intensity measures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjusting resident filing activity according to gross domestic product (GDP) and population helps when comparing the intensity of industrial design filing by residents across origins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: resident design count per USD 100 billion GDP and resident application design count per million population are used to show filing intensity; plotting per-capita vs GDP-per-capita can visualize intensity relative to development level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registrations in force estimation and age metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimating 'registrations in force' is done from data provided by offices (e.g., 136 offices provided data) and the average age of active registrations is reported per office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences in term lengths and office practices affect the number and average age of registrations in force; e.g., average age varies from 2.9 years (UK) to 10.3 years (Spain) in 2022.
